extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers (especially speculative fiction) who want to write or add humor
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and concrete techniques for making prose (novels, short stories, scenes) funny — with emphasis on speculative/genre fiction and keeping story/character while adding humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take expectations and twist them
rubrics_metrics.description: Set up an expectation and then break it in a surprising way to produce humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use established narrative expectations (genre tropes, character behavior, lists) and subvert the expected outcome; the rule of three is a common structure to set expectation and then deliver a twist on the third item. Play the twist so it also reveals something about character when useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be the anodyne for the evening news (humor's purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim to cheer or comfort readers — provide a pleasant counterpoint to bad news or daily stress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Position your work as light relief: craft tone and jokes that lift mood without being cruel for cruelty's sake. This is a guiding goal that affects choice of targets, gentleness of satire, and whether humor is inclusive (laughing with) or exclusive (laughing at).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggeration
rubrics_metrics.description: Amplify traits, situations, or stakes beyond realism to create comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make characters or circumstances larger-than-life (e.g., overprivileged aristocrats) so their foibles are visible and funny. Balance exaggeration with believable stakes if the story still needs emotional weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tweak or parody standard tropes
rubrics_metrics.description: Take common genre tropes (e.g., space opera) and make small, clever alterations that expose their absurdities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You don't need to abandon the trope — a gentle tweak often yields comedy. Use familiarity with the trope so the audience recognizes the deviation. Ensure the story can still function seriously if needed; humor can sit atop a real plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use (or break) the rule of three
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a list-of-three structure where the third item subverts expectation to produce humor, or intentionally break the rule for an effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct two items that set a pattern and make the third incongruous as a punchline. Alternatively, deliberately violate the rule of three to create surprise. Consider how the choice of the third item also reveals character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benign-violation positioning (move boundary between violation and benign)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make humor by positioning material so it overlaps between 'violation' (taboo/harmful) and 'benign' (safe), producing a laugh rather than shock.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shift details, tone, or distance so that something potentially offensive becomes acceptable to laugh at. Use the overlap carefully: too much violation is offensive, too much benign is boring. The podcast describes this as moving the circles to create overlap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy = tragedy + time/distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Material that was tragic can become funny given enough time or emotional/diegetic distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the worst bits out of immediate view (offstage) or place them far enough away in time/setting so the audience can laugh. Use distance to allow audience detachment; do not trivialize harm inappropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Puns as an intellectual form of humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Puns require the reader to understand multiple meanings/context and are an intellectual joke form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use puns when the book's tone and audience will appreciate wordplay; they demand context and can alienate some readers. Place puns deliberately and sparingly if you want them to land.

rubrics_metrics.name: Juxtapose modern elements with ancient or fantastic (anachronism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Place contemporary ideas, behaviors, or devices into historical or fantastical settings to create humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples like Shakespeare in Love show how modern rituals or language inserted into past settings can be charmingly funny; do it with care so the anachronism feels intentional and illuminates character or theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absurdities and anachronisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Embrace absurd situations and deliberate incongruities to produce comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let absurdity escalate in controlled ways; use it to highlight character or critique. Combine with other techniques (exaggeration, juxtaposition) for layered humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use prose timing and punctuation for comic timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Manage the reader's breathing and expectation using punctuation, italics, spacing, and page turns to create timing similar to spoken comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ellipses, m-dashes, italics, and forcing a page turn before a punchline can create pauses and beats. Treat written timing deliberately: set up a pause, land the line, then continue with a benign follow-up so readers laugh without missing plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure the line after the punchline carries story (be benign but informative)
rubrics_metrics.description: After a joke, follow with a line that keeps the narrative moving so laughter doesn't cause the reader to miss important information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the post-punchline sentence neutral/benign yet functional. That lets readers enjoy the joke and still follow plot or character development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine humor with serious story elements (maintain arcs and plot)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good humorous fiction still requires character arcs, plot, and literary styling — humor should not replace story craftsmanship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat humor as an added layer: maintain stakes, development, and emotional truth. Humor should enhance, not undercut, the reader's investment in the characters and story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use varied kinds of humor to reach different readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ multiple humor types (puns, anachronism, exaggeration, situational, character-based) because not every joke lands for every reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mix techniques so various audience members find something funny. Avoid relying on a single joke type that may alienate segments of your readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character-based humor (let character create comedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let a character's contradictions, sensibilities, and consistent foibles generate humor organically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build comedic personalities (e.g., feckless aristocrats, earnest straight-men) whose predictable reactions produce laughs. Use character detail and consistency so jokes feel earned and reveal deeper character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slapstick is difficult in prose; adapt with other devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical slapstick translates poorly to written form, so use alternative techniques to imply physical comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where slapstick would work on stage/screen, in prose rely on descriptive timing, phrasing, pacing (line breaks, sentence length), and the reader's imagination to evoke the physical humor instead of attempting cinematic choreography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give trivial things absurdly high stakes for comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign outsized importance to otherwise small or trivial matters to create humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat mundane objects or concerns as if they were of cosmic consequence (e.g., overly ceremonial obsession with a hobby) to highlight absurdity and create comedic conflict.
